answer_summary: Holekamp described the prior 15 years as anti-VEGF 1.0, dominated by regular intravitreal ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab. She said anti-VEGF 2.0 would mean more durable therapies and new anti-VEGF delivery concepts.

answer_summary: She saw PDS as the near-term approval candidate after ARCHWAY because it continuously delivered ranibizumab for 6 months with efficacy equivalent to monthly ranibizumab and a major reduction in treatment burden. She noted phase 3 completion in wet AMD and ongoing phase 3 programs in DME and DR.
answer_limitations: Written before PDS approval and later postmarketing safety events.

answer_summary: She interpreted the PDS patient-preference data as strongly favorable, saying the preference for PDS over injections was overwhelming and consistent with what she saw in practice.

answer_summary: She ranked phase 3-ready agents as the next durability advances, highlighting faricimab for dual VEGF/Ang2 targeting and possible 16-week wet AMD dosing. She also called KSI-301 promising based on early durability data across wet AMD, DME, and RVO, while noting it was still moving toward pivotal trials.
answer_limitations: Historical 2021 expectations; later evidence may differ, especially for KSI-301.

answer_summary: She was intrigued by gene-derived anti-VEGF as an advanced long-term concept and pointed to early positive wet AMD data from Adverum and Regenxbio. Her enthusiasm was cautious, emphasizing that the field still had a long way to go before a possible one-and-done approach.
answer_limitations: Historical early-stage gene-therapy view; not a current assessment of later trial outcomes.

answer_summary: For GA, she focused on slowing lesion growth and limiting vision loss rather than cure, comparing GA management conceptually to glaucoma. She highlighted complement inhibition programs from Apellis and Iveric, plus earlier factor H and factor I approaches from Gemini and Gyroscope, and also noted early non-complement approaches from Lineage and Stealth.
answer_limitations: GA-focused and historical; several programs have changed since 2021.

answer_summary: She was skeptical that oral or topical therapies would be the answer for retinal disease, citing the failed phase 3 wet AMD eye-drop program from Ohr as a cautionary example.
answer_limitations: Broad retina statement; not limited to wet AMD.

answer_summary: She expected adoption to vary between early adopters and more conservative physicians, but believed retina specialists have the surgical skill set to master PDS and other new delivery approaches. answer_summary: Holekamp called PDS a paradigm shift because it surgically implants a refillable ranibizumab reservoir that can be exchanged every 6 months. She emphasized strong patient appeal, 93% patient preference for PDS over injections in trial experience, noninferiority to monthly ranibizumab in ARCHWAY, and the need to treat it as effective but surgically different technology.

answer_summary: She viewed faricimab as anti-VEGF 2.0 because it targets VEGF plus the angiopoietin pathway, bringing retina closer to multi-pathway treatment models. She thought TENAYA/LUCERNE validated the second target by preserving noninferior vision and drying with less frequent dosing, and she was especially interested in whether year 2 would sustain 12- to 16-week intervals.

answer_summary: For incomplete responders, she first revisits the diagnosis and considers masqueraders such as central serous choroidopathy or adult vitelliform dystrophy. If convinced it is AMD, she may check response at 2 to 3 weeks, identifies high-VEGF-need patients who may require monthly injections, uses maintenance/treat-and-extend to preserve gains, and prioritizes eradicating intraretinal fluid more than subretinal fluid.

answer_summary: She was impressed that YOSEMITE/RHINE showed better anatomic drying than she expected, with a clearer anatomic difference between aflibercept and faricimab. She interpreted this as possible clinical validation that targeting a second pathway may help patients with diabetes, while waiting for year 2 data to clarify the magnitude and durability of the difference.
answer_limitations: DME-focused rather than wet AMD; edited transcript and 1-year data context.

answer_summary: She argued that visual acuity can miss GA burden because patients with foveal sparing may read well on an eye chart while struggling with reading, driving, contrast, and daily function. She said clinicians should listen closely to patients, recognize that contrast sensitivity and dark adaptation are not routinely captured, and use low-vision referrals when appropriate.
answer_limitations: GA-focused; multi-speaker edited transcript.

answer_summary: She agreed that binary labels like fast/slow and wet/dry can confuse patients and clinicians, because patients can have wet and dry AMD together. Her main referral concern was that community clinicians who readily refer wet AMD based on OCT fluid may miss or struggle to diagnose GA, especially early GA on OCT.
answer_limitations: GA-focused; answer is embedded in panel discussion about referral education.

answer_summary: She described GA as a relentless progressive disease that can take away reading, driving, independence, mood, and family roles, even when it is the patient's main health problem.
